passage:
"Why does Chintu get the mango kulfi and I get nothing?" Kamal muttered.
"Because his throat is sore and the doctor said cold things soothe it," said his mother, Rukmini, sitting down next to him.
"You have been quiet all week."
"Everybody asks about Chintu. Nobody asks about me." Then, quickly, "I feel bad saying that."
"You can feel both, Kamal."
"Can we go for a walk, just us, on Saturday?"
"Yes. And you can help me carry his soup tray, if you like."
Kamal nodded. "I do want him better."

qa.q: What did Kamal say he felt bad saying?
qa.a: He said everyone asks about Chintu and nobody asks about him.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling when he says, "I do want him better"?
qa.a: He still cares about his brother even though he felt jealous; the sentence shows love and guilt mixed with his earlier resentment.

qa.q: What small step did Kamal ask for that could help him?
qa.a: He asked for a walk with his mother on Saturday, a bit of one-on-one time, which lets him keep caring for his brother without losing his own place.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Kamal's complaint?
qa.a: Kamal's mother probably sees it as a normal reaction of a child who feels overlooked, and not as selfishness. She answers calmly and offers time and a task.

grounding: A child jealous of his sick brother's attention says so, feels guilty, and asks his mother for time; both feelings are accepted.

passage: Last winter my brother Siddharth had bad asthma attacks, and our whole house turned around him. Mummy slept in his room. Papa rushed home early with his medicines. Nobody came to my annual day, where I was the lead tree in the play. I'm Bhavna, and I remember thinking, I wish I were sick too. Then I felt awful, because some nights Siddharth could hardly breathe. One evening I told Papa both things: that I was jealous, and that I felt terrible for being jealous. He didn't get angry. He said both feelings made sense. After that, Papa and I had Sunday mornings for just the two of us, making poha together. And I read comics to Siddharth when he was stuck in bed.

qa.q: What part did Bhavna play at annual day?
qa.a: The lead tree in the play.

qa.q: What two feelings did Bhavna have about Siddharth's illness?
qa.a: Jealous of all the attention he got, and then guilty for feeling that while he could hardly breathe.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do with those feelings?
qa.a: Bhavna told Papa honestly, got Sunday mornings alone with him, and still read comics to Siddharth.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt hearing Bhavna's confession?
qa.a: Understanding, and perhaps sorry Bhavna had felt left out, since he said both feelings made sense and made time for them.

grounding: A child feels jealous of a sick brother's attention and then guilty, asks a parent for time, and still cares for the brother.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 4C, Wednesday.
During art, the class made get-well cards for Harish, Raghav's younger brother, who has been in hospital for two weeks. Raghav drew nothing. When I asked, he muttered, 'Everyone's always making things for Harish. Nobody even asked about my football final.' Then his face went red and he covered it. 'I'm horrible. He's sick and I'm jealous.' I told him that jealous and guilty can sit side by side in anyone, and neither makes him bad. I suggested he tell his parents he misses time with them. He decided to make Harish a card with a football on it, 'so he knows about my final too.' I have emailed his mother about our chat.

qa.q: How long has Harish been in hospital?
Why did Raghav cover his red face?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and guilty for being jealous of Harish while Harish was sick.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest, and what did Raghav decide?
qa.a: To tell his parents he misses time with them; Raghav chose to make Harish a card with a football on it.

qa.q: How might Harish feel getting a football card from Raghav?
qa.a: Happy and included, hearing about his brother's final even from hospital.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy admitting jealousy and guilt about his sick brother, and turning it into care.
